rationale: Both responses cover the main options with pros, cons and longevity notes, and reach similar conclusions on the longevity bonus: open-source, community-owned tools such as Phaser, Three.js and Godot are the safest bets, and Unity's web export is the risk. B is more accurate and better organized. It groups engines into 2D, 3D and cross-platform tools with web export. It correctly separates Babylon.js, a full engine with physics and input, from Three.js, a rendering library, whereas A lumps them together and wrongly says you build everything yourself in both. B also adds PixiJS, an important foundational 2D renderer. A has several factual slips: Construct's engine is not open-source, PlayCanvas is not strictly 3D-only, and the Cocos ownership claim is shaky. B has its own error, the claim that melonJS is built on LimeJS, and its 'avoid Unity WebGL' advice is a bit blunt. A usefully includes a no-code option in Construct. On balance B's structure and higher accuracy make it the better answer.
